title: The Baltic Withdrawal
subtitle: Tallinn’s evacuation, survival at sea and the limits of Soviet authority
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: The loss of Tallinn left ships and passengers facing unequal chances of escape. The study follows minefields, rescue, resistance to forced evacuation, the persecution of Jews left ashore and Finland’s advance on the Karelian Isthmus.
body:
A port lost and a fleet still at sea

On 29 August 1941, ships from Tallinn were scattered across an unfinished withdrawal. Some were approaching Kronstadt; others still faced mines and German aircraft. Soldiers, sailors, wounded men, families and forcibly mobilised Estonians had left the port the previous day. For passengers on damaged vessels, the next destination might be an island, a rescue boat or the water. Tallinn’s capture had ended the land battle, but survival at sea still depended on protection and rescue after the main naval force had passed.[1]

The problem had developed on land. German forces reached the coast east of Tallinn near Kunda on 7 August, cutting the overland connection between the Soviet troops around the Estonian capital and the main body of the 8th Army farther east. Tallinn remained a naval base with substantial coastal artillery, but it was increasingly a defended enclosure. Vice Admiral Vladimir Tributs commanded the Baltic Fleet; Major General Ivan Nikolayev’s 10th Rifle Corps provided the principal army headquarters for its land defence. German General Georg von Küchler’s 18th Army approached through Estonia. The fight therefore joined two military systems: a field army trying to reduce a coastal position and a naval command using ships and shore batteries to sustain soldiers whose landward communications had been severed.[2]a

At Tallinn, the army’s survival depended on transferring a fighting force from land to sea while its rearguard remained under attack. Loading took time that the defenders had to buy. Heavy weapons could protect the quays until late in the withdrawal, yet their crews still needed a way aboard. Harbour staff had to connect particular units with particular ships through streets whose accessibility was changing. These were the terms of the Soviet decision to leave: enough order had to survive for men to embark and, after landing, to fight again.

For Estonians, the word evacuation requires particular care. Soviet occupation and annexation in 1940 had already transformed the political meaning of military authority, a background established in the atlas’s study of the August 1939 pact. In summer 1941, men could be ordered aboard under compulsory mobilisation rather than choosing to leave. Others travelled because they feared the approaching Germans, because their employment connected them to the Soviet administration, or because they were wounded and dependent on military transport. These categories overlapped aboard the same vessels. A ship’s passenger total cannot tell us whether those passengers understood its departure as rescue, duty, displacement or coercion.[3]b

The narrowing land perimeter

The German assault began on 20 August along the approaches to Tallinn. The 254th Infantry Division advanced through the coastal sector and along the Narva road, the 61st followed the Tartu road and railway, and the 217th operated farther southwest. Colonel Rudolf Friedrich’s separate group included troops from the 291st Division. Only parts of some divisions were committed. The corps reports reproduced by the Estonian War Museum trace their progress through junctions, river positions and assembled detachments, rather than four complete divisions advancing abreast.[2]

The northern approach demonstrates how progress could change within a short distance. German troops reached Kuusalu and Kahala on 20 August and pressed towards the Jägala system. As they drew closer to Tallinn, however, they entered the effective reach of naval and coastal guns. On 26 August, the 254th Division’s advance near Iru encountered resistance around the Pirita River and the heights east of the city. The defenders could draw upon heavy weapons whose position at the coast made them difficult for an advancing infantry regiment to silence. Such fire did not restore a land route to Leningrad. It did make the final approach more costly and helped keep the evacuation window open.[2]

A report by Major Oskar Muehlenberg on the fighting at Kiviloo on 22 August offers a more intimate view of the same operational friction. His battalion of the 61st Division had to work through restricted roads, woods and wet ground. Reconnaissance, artillery and machine guns preceded the infantry’s movement; a bridgehead was established near Peningi, but the arrival of another battalion became a condition for continuing the advance. Muehlenberg also noted shortages of experienced junior leaders. This contemporary German report, reproduced and examined by historian Toomas Hiio, records a successful attack without making it effortless. Its estimates of Soviet losses remain the attacker’s claims, while its account of waiting for supporting troops explains why a local breakthrough did not automatically become a rapid pursuit.[4]c

The Soviet corps account describes the opposite side of that pressure. By the final days, units covered road junctions and principal approaches while wide intervals opened between their positions. Its report attributed severe weakness to losses among platoon, company and battalion commanders, with junior personnel taking over formations larger than their normal responsibilities. It also recorded the use of an antiaircraft unit in an antitank role and the loss of most of its weapons. These statements should be read as a headquarters explaining its defeat, but they identify concrete mechanisms of deterioration: the disappearance of experienced leaders, the diversion of specialist weapons and the inability to maintain a continuous defensive line.[2]

On 27 August the pressure reached the city’s working infrastructure. German reports describe fighting towards the northeastern districts and the approaches to the harbour. Factories, houses and prepared positions impeded the advance, while Soviet artillery still covered the withdrawal. The corps headquarters divided its remaining defence between southern and eastern sectors, the latter including a mixture of riflemen, naval infantry, border troops and remnants of other units under Colonel Terenti Parafilo. These were not interchangeable reserves. They had different weapons, training and organisational histories, and their concentration around a shrinking perimeter did not necessarily produce a coherent fighting force. The withdrawal plan had to make them reach assigned ships while they were still disengaging from combat.[2]

The German returns also place limits on the language of easy conquest. The 254th Division reported 396 killed and 1,576 wounded between 20 and 29 August. Those figures describe one division over a defined period, not the losses of the entire 18th Army or a count confined to the final street fighting. The division then moved towards the Leningrad front. Its next assignment therefore began with a loss of trained personnel that a map of newly conquered territory would not show. Replacements, where available, still had to reach companies, learn their immediate tasks and restore the working relationships on which infantry attacks depended. The Soviet defence had failed to preserve Tallinn, but its effect on the attacking force survived the city’s fall.[2]d

Embarkation as a battle of communications

The corps report places the distribution of embarkation instructions at 11.30 on 27 August and the beginning of disengagement in the early afternoon. Loading then became entangled with the destruction of the base itself. According to this account, the Baltic Fleet headquarters building was demolished prematurely, taking with it the central telephone exchange used by both the fleet and the corps. Communications with units broke down during the evening, and messengers had to replace the damaged network. That was more than a headquarters inconvenience. An order changing a ship’s berth had to reach a battalion moving through streets under fire, and its new destination had to remain recognisable when earlier instructions were already circulating.[2]

Artillery fire against the Old Harbour forced transports to shift towards Bekker Harbour. The resulting changes affected particular units, not simply an anonymous mass of evacuees. The 204th Rifle Regiment, the 140th Howitzer Regiment and portions of the naval infantry were among the troops directed towards reassigned vessels. Other groups had to move to the Mine Harbour or the harbour of the former Russo-Baltic works. The report acknowledges that some commanders did not receive the revised instructions. An evacuation plan therefore existed, but the communications needed to execute it were being dismantled at the moment of greatest dependence upon them. The evidence supports criticism of that sequence without requiring the claim that every part of the withdrawal was chaotic.[2]

The damaged communications system did not prevent the whole evacuation. The corps account describes much of the main body embarking within several hours, protected by naval gunfire, with further concentrations continuing into the night. Rearguards followed, sometimes using small boats to reach ships offshore. These arrangements saved thousands, while failures to deliver revised instructions left other men without a vessel. At the level of an individual unit, escape could depend on whether its route, berth and assigned ship were still connected by a working order.[2]e

A departure that did not mean consent

Väino Laasnurm remembered leaving on Alev with other Estonian mobilised men while the Estonian anthem was sung. His later account, preserved by the Estonian Maritime Museum, also recalled naval mines carried aboard the transport. The departure was imposed by Soviet authority, yet the passengers retained attachments to the country they were leaving. Laasnurm’s recollection gives one man’s experience of that coercion; it cannot establish the wishes of everyone aboard. Preserving manpower for the Soviet war effort could mean carrying people away against their will.[3]f

The Soviet naval instructions of 1940 placed an escorted transport movement under a convoy commander and defined the authority of naval commandants aboard transports. Embarked army commanders were subordinate within this arrangement during the passage. The rules addressed a real danger: a ship’s captain, a senior army passenger and a distant headquarters could otherwise issue incompatible instructions. At Tallinn, the formal hierarchy remained dependent on signals, identifiable vessels and troops reaching the correct berth. No regulation could reconnect the demolished exchange or deliver an instruction to a unit that had already moved. [5]g

Minefields, escorts and unequal journeys

The eastward withdrawal assembled into several transport convoys and separate naval groups. Tributs travelled with the principal warships, including the cruiser Kirov; other groups provided cover and the rearguard. The German naval chronology compiled by Jürgen Rohwer and Gerhard Hümmelchen identifies four transport convoys and distinguishes them from these fighting formations. This organisation matters because the fate of a fast destroyer cannot stand for that of a loaded merchant vessel. Warships possessed their own combinations of speed, compartmentalisation, armament and trained crews. Transports carried the people whom the evacuation was intended to save but could not necessarily keep pace with the ships protecting them.[1]

The main danger was concentrated around the mine barriers near Cape Juminda. German and Finnish minelaying had turned part of the gulf into an obstacle that could be crossed only with serious risk and limited sweeping capacity. Aircraft added another threat, particularly to ships moving slowly or unable to maintain formation. Passing the mine barriers required more than knowing their general location. Minesweepers had to establish navigable passages, and the following ships needed to remain within those passages while avoiding collision, attack and disabled vessels. A vessel could possess enough fuel to reach Kronstadt and still lack a safe lane through which to use it. Here, the scarce logistical resource was navigable water under protection.[1]h

The navy’s 1937 and 1940 regulations show what safe passage demanded. They prescribed mine watches and warnings between ships, distinguished routine clearance near a base from exposed sweeping operations, and required protection for the minesweepers themselves. A workable plan also needed reconnaissance, suitable equipment and enough time for the available force to clear a route. These requirements explain why minesweeping was more than an escort sailing ahead of a convoy. A disabled sweeper or a vessel drifting out of the cleared passage could disrupt the movement of many ships behind it. [5]

The withdrawal’s planners had to weigh risks that could not all be reduced together. An earlier departure might leave intended passengers ashore; a slower passage might aid navigation but prolong exposure to aircraft. Available vessels, knowledge of the minefields and the protection that could be provided limited the choices. Communications failures during embarkation added avoidable difficulties to the dangers at sea. The losses alone cannot establish that a safe alternative was available.[5]i

The night of 28–29 August brought heavy mine losses. On 29 August the surviving movement separated further as faster naval vessels continued towards Kronstadt and vulnerable transports faced additional air attacks. Islands offered refuge for some people whose ships were sinking or damaged, but reaching an island was not the same as reaching the Soviet base. Rescue craft operating around Suursaari, also known as Gogland or Hogland, recovered survivors over subsequent days. Consequently, a chronological account must follow rescue as well as destruction. Counting only the ships arriving with the main force omits people temporarily stranded, while counting later rescues as additional passengers can duplicate individuals already included in broader evacuation totals.[1]j

People between the totals

Tallinn’s evacuation totals cover different people, voyages and periods. R. A. Zubkov’s naval study shows how calculations can change when they include transport crews, embarked troops, naval personnel or civilians on different terms. A count of the late-August breakout cannot simply be substituted for a figure covering voyages throughout August and September. These incompatible definitions prevent a dependable single death toll for everything described as the Tallinn evacuation.[5]

The Estonian Maritime Museum similarly treats the evacuation across a wider period. Its discussion distinguishes people who died, people who survived the loss of their ships and people eventually delivered to Kronstadt. Those categories cannot simply be added together: a shipwreck survivor might subsequently belong among the arrivals. The same caution applies to mobilised Estonians who disappeared from Soviet records but escaped or returned to Estonian territory. An absence in one army’s accounting can establish that a man did not reach his assigned destination; it does not establish by itself that he died. Reconstructing individual fates demands comparison between ship records, mobilisation lists, island landings and later testimony.[6]k

Heino Niidas and the work of staying afloat

Heino Niidas was eighteen when he survived the sinking of Sibir on an earlier August evacuation voyage. He later told an interviewer that a lifeboat took water after being lowered unevenly, and that he eventually clung to a long piece of timber with another man. By the time help arrived, cold and exhaustion had left him unable to grip the means offered to pull him aboard; he remembered holding a rope between his teeth. His account concerns that earlier voyage, not the main departure of 28 August. It shows how rescue remained physically difficult even after someone had escaped a sinking ship.[6]l

A different outcome followed the bombing of Eestirand on 24 August. The Estonian War Museum records passengers demanding to land despite an order to continue towards Kronstadt. The political officer and naval cadets threatened them but did not prevent Captain Boris Nelke from bringing the ship to Prangli. On 29 August, mobilised men led by reserve Captain Martin Grosberger seized control on the island and disarmed Soviet sailors, who were handed to the Germans the next day. This was a documented local resistance to compulsory service and evacuation, not evidence of a mutiny throughout the fleet.[7]m

The military consequences likewise extended beyond a ship’s arrival. The 10th Rifle Corps records reproduced by the War Museum describe subsequent efforts to rebuild the 10th Rifle Division. On 4 September its staff requested men from the Kronstadt garrison; on 7 September further personnel were ordered into the reorganised division. An authorised establishment was a plan for the force to be created, not proof that it already possessed all those soldiers and weapons. Survivors returning without their former artillery or transport could contribute experience and manpower while still requiring substantial re-equipment. The evacuation preserved part of an army, but it delivered that part into another emergency whose demands began immediately.[2]

The corps report’s account of artillery losses adds a further qualification to the apparent success of rescuing manpower. A rifleman could be loaded into a small boat when a gun, ammunition wagon or workshop vehicle could not. The remaining artillery also had to continue covering embarkation until late in the withdrawal. Saving the men who served those weapons and saving their equipment could thus become competing tasks. Reconstituting a division near Leningrad required more than issuing a new organisational order: it meant finding weapons, ammunition, communications equipment and transport for men whose earlier formation had lost much of that material. Naval evacuation and land reinforcement were successive parts of one process, and the gap between them could be measured in fighting power as well as time.[2]n

For Jews left in Tallinn, German occupation brought a distinct danger. Meelis Maripuu documents arrests in late August and early September, before Sonderkommando 1a commander Martin Sandberger’s wider instructions of 10 September. Jews were separated from other prisoners on transfer to Tallinn Central Prison; the later instructions demanded the arrest of Jewish men over sixteen and confinement of women considered fit for work. These were persecutory categories. Maripuu distinguishes contemporary records from later interrogations and leaves some dates and totals unresolved. Arrest, forced labour and killing developed through the opening weeks of occupation, rather than occurring on a single day when the fleet departed.[8]o

Finland’s advance and the question of an exit

North of the gulf, the Finnish advance had its own objectives and command structure. Viipuri, or Vyborg, was recaptured on 29 August. Its recovery carried considerable national significance after Finland’s territorial losses in the Winter War, but the operation also changed the military approaches to Leningrad. Finnish forces were conducting their own campaign under Marshal Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim; they were not simply another corps of Küchler’s army. Separate command, however, did not make their operations unrelated to Germany’s war. The pressure they exerted forced Soviet forces to defend another direction while the German advance threatened the city from the south.[9]

Historian Mikko Karjalainen’s reconstruction follows the cooperation and friction between the Finnish II and IV Corps. The former reached the Vuoksi at Kiviniemi on 23 August; Lieutenant General Lennart Oesch’s IV Corps sought to turn the defences of Viipuri and interrupt withdrawal towards the southeast. A crossing of Viipuri Bay enlarged the operation beyond its initial conception. Yet attempted encirclement did not prevent substantial Soviet escape, and the desire to enter the city could compete with the less visible task of blocking routes beyond it. In early September the Finnish advance on the Isthmus approached its limit; Mannerheim’s order to assume the defensive followed on 4 September. Karjalainen places command difficulties and losses within that decision, warning against an account in which effortless success was halted solely by political restraint.[10]p

Private diplomacy shows how uncertain Finland’s relationship with the wider war remained. On 18 August, American Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles told Finnish minister Hjalmar Procopé that the Soviet government was prepared to discuss peace with territorial concessions. Welles stressed that Washington was transmitting information rather than presenting a completed settlement. Procopé raised the problem of guarantees: after Finland’s experience of Soviet power, how could an arrangement be made durable? Welles in turn questioned whether German predominance would provide a reliable guarantee of Finnish independence. The exchange concerned competing dangers and possible diplomatic exits, not a peace agreement that Finland could simply have signed on terms already fixed.[11]

A report from Helsinki three days later records Foreign Minister Rolf Witting considering whether Finland might leave active war after securing its strategic aims, perhaps following a German occupation of Leningrad. American minister H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld also recorded uncertainty about whether Germany would permit such a withdrawal. These were contemporary political calculations, not a subsequent historian’s proof that every Finnish operation served a single settled plan. They disclose the tension between an aspiration to limit Finland’s war and dependence upon a German victory large enough to make that limitation seem possible. The expectations themselves had consequences for Soviet assessments of the northern threat.[12]q

By 29 August, Soviet power had lost Tallinn but retained ships, crews and soldiers who could contribute to Leningrad’s defence. Their usefulness depended on landing, reorganisation and equipment, while rescue work remained unfinished. Finland’s recovery of Viipuri had meanwhile increased pressure on the northern approaches. For Estonian passengers, reaching a Soviet base and escaping Soviet authority could be very different outcomes; for Jews left ashore, German occupation brought a distinct and escalating danger. The Soviet Counterstroke turns to Yelnya, where another Soviet command was trying to force the Germans to relinquish ground.
